questions.prompt: A CS device with \(g_m = 4\ \mathrm{mS}\) has \(R_S = 1\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) in its source (\(r_o\) and body effect ignored). Find the effective transconductance \(G_m = i_{out}/v_{in}\) in mS.
questions.explanation: \(G_m = g_m/(1 + g_mR_S) = 4/(1 + 4) = 0.8\ \mathrm{mS}\). The source resistor feeds back: current through it raises \(v_s\) and cuts \(v_{gs}\).

questions.prompt: Why add source degeneration to a CS stage?
options: Its gain and linearity depend less on the transistor's \(g_m\)
To reduce the DC current to zero
questions.explanation: For \(g_mR_S \gg 1\), \(G_m \to 1/R_S\), set by a resistor. Gain falls, but becomes predictable and linear.

questions.prompt: With the gate at AC ground, find the resistance (kΩ) looking into the drain of a device with \(g_m = 2\ \mathrm{mS}\), \(r_o = 50\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) and \(R_S = 2\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\).
questions.explanation: \(R_{out} = r_o + R_S + g_mr_oR_S = 50 + 2 + 200 = 252\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\). The reader's Eq. 13.10 drops the lone \(R_S\), fine when \(g_mR_S\) is large.

questions.prompt: A degenerated CS stage has \(g_m = 5\ \mathrm{mS}\), \(R_S = 500\ \Omega\) and \(R_D = 10\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) (\(r_o\) ignored). Find the voltage gain. (\(A_v = -G_mR_D\) uses the CS analysis as a labelled step.)
questions.explanation: \(G_m = 5/(1 + 2.5) = 1.43\ \mathrm{mS}\), so \(A_v = -14.3\), roughly \(-R_D/R_S = -20\) and approaching it as \(g_m\) grows.

questions.prompt: In a degenerated stage with \(g_mR_S = 4\), you double \(R_S\). What happens to \(G_m\)?
options: It falls by about 44%, from \(g_m/5\) to \(g_m/9\)
questions.explanation: \(G_m = g_m/(1 + g_mR_S)\): \(1/5\) to \(1/9\) is a 44% drop. It halves exactly only in the limit \(g_mR_S \gg 1\).
